entities.name: All-Ukrainian Union of Churches of Evangelical Christians-Baptists
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The All-Ukrainian Union of Churches of Evangelical Christians-Baptists (VUTSEHB), the largest Protestant denomination in Ukraine with approximately 2,500 churches and 120,000+ members, traces its roots to the 19th-century Baptist and Evangelical movements that emerged in the Russian Empire's Ukrainian territories despite tsarist persecution — and has survived Soviet repression (including Stalin's near-liquidation of its leadership in the 1930s), forced union with state-controlled religious councils, and now operates in the context of Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Baptist Christianity spread to the Ukrainian territories of the Russian Empire in the 1860s-1870s through German colonist communities in the south (particularly around Odessa) and through indigenous revival movements. The movement grew despite periodic tsarist persecution; after the 1917 Revolution, Baptists briefly enjoyed religious freedom before Stalin's terror decimated Baptist and Evangelical leadership in the 1930s with mass arrests and executions.

During the Soviet era, Ukraine's Baptists faced the choice of registering with the state-controlled All-Union Council of Evangelical Christians-Baptists (a government oversight body) or facing illegality — a compromise that many communities accepted but some 'unregistered' or 'underground' congregations rejected. After Ukrainian independence (1991), the All-Ukrainian Union emerged as the main successor body, navigating post-Soviet religious pluralism. Since 2022, Ukrainian Baptist churches have been actively involved in humanitarian assistance to displaced civilians and in supporting Ukrainian soldiers, giving the denomination a new national-service profile in wartime Ukraine.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The All-Ukrainian Union of Evangelical Christians-Baptists — surviving tsarist persecution, Stalinist terror, Soviet control, and now supporting Ukraine during Russia's 2022 invasion — is a resilient Protestant institution whose history maps the arc of religious freedom in Eastern Europe from empire to independence.
